iconicAnchor.label: Mount Lebanon Shaker workrooms, peg rails, storage furniture, chairs, and useful objects
iconicAnchor.creatorOrTradition: United Society of Believers, especially the Mount Lebanon Shaker community
iconicAnchor.whyCanonical: Shaker Museum situates furniture, baskets, boxes, brooms, agriculture, manufacturing, and design within the community's religious, social, and entrepreneurial life rather than treating plain objects as anonymous rustic style.

sources.title: The Shakers
supports: Shaker craft and manufacturing belonged to a specific communal religious society whose members made furniture, baskets, brooms, boxes, and other useful goods.
Usefulness, innovation, communal life, and rejection of the superfluous are central context for interpreting the material culture.

sources.title: The wonderful world of joinery
supports: Shaker woodworkers used precise mortise-and-tenon, dovetail, dado, and other joints to make strong useful furniture and architectural fittings.
Threaded pegs and peg boards demonstrate a distinctive union of repeated visual order, practical maintenance, and mechanical invention.

culturalContext.note: Present Shaker Utility as the material culture of a named American religious community. Ground visual choices in documented daily work, communal order, practical invention, and museum-held objects; avoid costume figures, generalized Christian symbolism, farmhouse nostalgia, and claims that plain wood alone is Shaker.
